abstract: Fibroblasts are readily obtained and expanded and may provide an alternative cell source for cultivated seafood if their latent myogenic potential can be accessed. We examined whether transient exposure to 5-azacytidine (AZA), a cytidine analogue known to convert mouse embryonic fibroblasts into myoblasts, elicits a persistent muscle gene program in embryo-derived zebrafish (Danio rerio) Z3 fibroblasts. Cells were exposed to 0, 2.5, 5 or 10 M AZA for 48 h and maintained in drug-free medium for 3 weeks. RNA-seq identified 744 genes that increased and 670 that decreased consistently across the concentration series. Increased genes encompassed myogenic regulators, fusion factors, sarcomeric components and excitation-contraction machinery, whereas decreased genes were enriched for extracellular-matrix and adhesion functions. In a separate six-dose RT-qPCR experiment (0-20 M AZA) with three biological replicates per concentration, all 19 selected muscle genes were significantly increased at 1.25 M, the lowest concentration tested, whereas 9 of 12 extracellular-matrix/fibroblast genes were significantly decreased. Several muscle genes plateaued or declined at higher concentrations, and multinucleated myotubes were not observed. A separate 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine (decitabine) series showed a comparable muscle-associated response at 0.25 M. These findings indicate that zebrafish fibroblasts retain access to a myogenic-like transcriptional program, and they provide a model for identifying food-compatible approaches to control fish-cell lineage plasticity for cultivated seafood.
